title: Customer POC network design sprint notes
content:
Purpose:
Runbook-style sprint notes from the week-long networking design sprint for Customer X POC. This doc captures tradeoffs evaluated, test plan fragments, DNS and endpoint patterns we recommended, and immediate action items for the next workshop. These are working notes — expect follow-ups and a cleaned architecture proposal later.

Context and constraints (customer-specific):
- Customer X requires a VPC-isolated deployment in their AWS account for data residency.
- No inbound public IPs on model inference hosts (strict egress-only policy).
- Must support both hosted-redwood control plane callbacks (HTTPS) and private ingestion from customer systems.
- Auditable network flow logs and KMS-integrated key management for TLS certs.
- Expected bursty inference load (1000 qps peak) with short tail latency SLOs (p95 < 120ms).
- Limited customer ops experience with complex routing; prefer simpler operational patterns.

Assumptions we used in sizing and routing options:
- Inference nodes run in private subnets behind ENIs attached to an autoscaling group.
- Models are pinned to nodes via the runtime; KV caches are local.
- Customer will accept a small set of cross-account interface endpoints or VPC peering connections.

Candidate architectures considered (high level):
1) PrivateLink-first (Interface Endpoints)
   - Pros: No route-table changes, granular IAM/SG control, easier to register service names in customer DNS via interface endpoint IPs.
   - Cons: Increased per-ENI cost at high throughput; scaling the number of endpoints for many AZs can be operationally heavy.

2) VPC Peering with explicit routing (regional peering mesh)
   - Pros: Lower per-packet cost for high-volume east-west traffic, straightforward pathing for high-throughput inference.
   - Cons: No transitive routing; more route-table management across subnets and on-prem connectivity overhead.

3) Transit Gateway + Shared Services VPC
   - Pros: Centralized egress controls, supports multiple VPCs, easier multi-account scale.
   - Cons: Added cost and operational complexity; transitive routing needs careful security posture.

Design decision we settled on for the POC (interim):
- Use VPC Peering for control-plane <-> inference communication within region (customer account <-> redwood-managed account) to minimize latency and cost for token-heavy calls.
- Use Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) for sensitive billing/metadata APIs that require IAM-scoped per-service access and to reduce blast radius for third-party integrations.
- Keep egress via a customer-managed NAT Gateway (short-term) with a long-term option to move to an egress proxy running in a dedicated private-subnet autoscaling group (for connection reuse and TLS termination auditing).

DNS strategy (split-horizon + resolution patterns):
- Create a customer-private hosted zone (e.g., redwood.<customer>.internal) delegated to customer account. Redwood publishes CNAME entries pointing to interface endpoint DNS names where PrivateLink is used.
- For peering paths, we recommend adding explicit A-records in the private hosted zone that map service names to the peered IPs (tracked by a small automation script run during deployment).
- TTLs: keep low (60s) for POC to support quick rollback during rollouts.
- Fallback path: for any control-plane domain, set up a SaaS-backup DNS name that resolves to redwood-hosted public endpoints to be used only when peering is down (enforced via route table priority and health checks).

Egress control and outbound connectivity patterns:
- Short-term (fastest to get POC working): NAT Gateway per AZ for predictable SNAT, with VPC flow logs enabled to CloudWatch for auditing.
- Mid-term (recommended): Egress proxy (envoy) cluster in private subnets behind an internal ALB. Benefits: connection pooling to external services, mTLS termination for 3rd party webhook callbacks, and centralized TLS cert management tied to KMS.
- Long-term (compliant customers): Place egress through an on-prem firewall/VPN with static IPs for allowlisting by external partners.

Security groups and IAM patterns:
- Principle of least privilege: create one SG for control-plane traffic (only allow HTTPS from redwood control plane CIDRs) and one SG for metrics/telemetry (allow only outbound to monitoring endpoints).
- Use IAM roles for cross-account calls - avoid long-lived credentials. Documented pattern: redwood assumes a ReadOnly role to query metadata, customer supplies a short-lived role for provisioning endpoints.

Endpoints and service discovery details:
- PrivateLink service names: service.redwood-inference.ctrl.region.amazonaws.com (interface endpoint targets deployed in redwood account).
- For inference endpoints, use per-AZ target groups and a per-customer prefix in naming so security/route configs are scoped.

Testing & validation checklist (POC smoke tests):
- VPC peering: verify route table entries present in both VPCs and traceroute identifies direct peered hops.
- Private DNS: dig +search for redwood.<customer>.internal -> verifies resolves to internal IPs.
- Endpoint connectivity: curl --resolve against service name to ensure TLS handshake with customer-managed certs.
- Egress path verification: from inference host, curl to external webhook URL and confirm SNAT IP matches expected NAT egress IP.
- Flow logs: sample 10k packets over 15m and verify allow/deny behavior in logs.
- Latency baseline: run synthetic p50/p95 token generation against the deployed model with and without PrivateLink to quantify extra hop.

Operational runbook snippets (quick commands):
- Check peering status: aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters Name=tag:Customer,Values=<CUSTOMER>
- Dump route tables: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=<VPCID>
- Resolve private DNS from EC2: dig @169.254.169.253 redwood.<customer>.internal

Observed tradeoffs during the workshop (notes):
- PrivateLink added ~3–5ms median to control-plane calls under our lab load due to extra ENI hop; peering was lower latency but required more ops work to maintain route tables across multiple accounts.
- NAT Gateway costs were non-trivial at customer projected traffic; egress proxy gave us both cost and observability wins in projections, but needed more effort to harden.

Open questions to take to architecture review:
- For multi-region POC: do we keep Transit Gateway or prefer inter-region peering + per-region PrivateLink?
- How does customer want to handle certificate lifecycle for internal TLS between control plane and inference nodes (ACM? customer-owned cert? mTLS?)
- Sizing guidance for PrivateLink: at what qps should we switch away from Interface Endpoints to peering to control per-ENI cost?

Action items (owner — due):
- Diego: Draft cleaned architecture diagram and short delta doc comparing PrivateLink vs Peering for customer ops — due 2026-02-28.
- Priya: Prototype an envoy-based egress proxy example with config snippets for token auth and mTLS — due 2026-03-05.
- Alyssa: Automate private hosted zone A-record creation tied to deployment tags (repo PR with script) — due 2026-02-25.
- Jonah: Run cost simulation for NAT Gateway vs Egress Proxy at projected traffic volumes and summarize — due 2026-03-01.

Workshop retrospective (what worked / what to change):
- Worked: Hands-on lab with customer network team accelerated buy-in on peering + DNS patterns.
- To change: allocate 1/2 day to simulated failure modes (peering down, PrivateLink rate limits) in next workshop to validate fallback strategies.

Appendix: helpful snippet templates (to copy into deploy repo)
- Route table terraform snippet (example):
  resource "aws_route" "peer_to_redwood" {
    route_table_id = var.customer_route_table
    destination_cidr_block = var.redwood_vpc_cidr
    vpc_peering_connection_id = aws_vpc_peering_connection.peer.id
  }

- DNS automation (bash):
  aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id $ZONE --change-batch '{"Changes":[{"Action":"UPSERT","ResourceRecordSet":{"Name":"redwood.'$CUSTOMER'.internal","Type":"A","TTL":60,"ResourceRecords":[{"Value":"'$PEER_IP'"}]}}]}'

Notes for the final architecture proposal: keep this doc as working history. Final proposal should include: clear failure modes, costs per-month (NAT vs PrivateLink vs TGW), single-page DNS diagram, and a short runbook for on-call to triage network issues.

End of sprint notes.
